I suppose I do enjoy them a little once I’m there, but it’s not like it used to be. Choir used to lift me up, you know? I’ll sit at home with the TV on low, not really watching it, just letting it make noise in the room. Now most days I just end up sitting at home with the TV on low, not even really watching it all the time. I know people are expecting me, or that I ought to go, but I just… don’t get myself moving. It feels like the wanting is kind of dulled down.\n\nDoctor: Have you been feeling down or depressed?\n\nPatient: I don’t know if I’d call it depressed, exactly. I mean, I get quiet, and I sit around more than I used to, and some days feel kind of flat, like there’s not much spark in me. But “down” like crying all the time or feeling real sad… I’m not sure that’s it.\n\nIt’s more like things take too much out of me before I even start them. I’ll think, “I should go do that,” and then I just don’t. So I don’t know if that’s being depressed or just… I don’t know, worn out inside maybe.\n\nDoctor: Have you been having trouble with your memory?\n\nPatient: Memory… I’m not sure. I don’t think I’ve noticed anything big like that. I mean, I’ll walk into a room and forget what I went in there for, but I always figured everybody my age does that some. Or I’ll put my glasses down and then fuss around looking for them, and half the time they’re right on the table.\n\nBut as far as, you know, really not remembering people or getting lost or something… no, I don’t think so. At least nobody’s told me I’m forgetting things badly. Sometimes I don’t keep up with things because I don’t feel like doing them, but that feels different than memory to me.\n\nDoctor: About how long have you been feeling this way?\n\nPatient: It’s been… well, it didn’t just come on all at once. I’d say it’s been building since I retired from the school office. That was a little over two years ago now.\n\nAt first I thought it was just adjusting, you know, not having to get up and be somewhere, not having people coming by my desk or needing things from me. I figured I’d settle into retirement and find a rhythm. But over time it just sort of kept going that way, like I got less and less inclined to do the things I used to make myself do. So… a little over two years, I guess, if I’m being honest.\n\nDoctor: During this time, have you felt sad most days?\n\nPatient: Most days… I don’t know. I wouldn’t say sad exactly. Not like I wake up thinking, “Oh, I’m so sad,” or I’m crying into my coffee or anything like that. It’s more… blank, maybe. Quiet. Like the day is there and I’m there, but I don’t feel much about it one way or the other.\n\nSome days I do feel a little low, especially when I think about how I used to be busier and had more reason to get dressed and go out, but I’m not sure that’s sadness most days. It’s hard for me to name it. I just feel kind of slowed down and not very interested, but sad… I don’t know if that’s the right word.\n\nDoctor: Have you been having trouble managing your bills or other paperwork?\n\nPatient: Bills and paperwork… well, I try to keep the bills in the little basket by the phone, and I do usually get to them, eventually. I don’t know if I’d say it’s the bills exactly that are the worst.\n\nWhere I’ve noticed it more is with church things and the senior center. I used to help lead the choir, not just singing, but keeping track of who was coming, what music we were doing, little notes like that. And I helped with some of the senior-center projects too, making calls or bringing papers or saying I’d follow up with somebody. Lately I’ve had to step back from a lot of that because I’ll say, “Yes, I can do that,” and then I just don’t keep up the way I used to.\n\nIt’s embarrassing, honestly, because people were used to relying on me. Now some of the ladies from church check on me more than they used to, like they’ll call and say, “Did you remember we’re meeting?” or “Do you still have that paper?” They’re kind about it, but I can tell they’re watching out for me a little more. So… paperwork at home, I manage some, but keeping up with responsibilities and things I promised people has gotten harder.\n\nDoctor: Do you still enjoy things like choir or quilting when you actually do them?\n\nPatient: I suppose I do enjoy them a little once I’m there, but it’s not like it used to be. Choir used to lift me up, you know? I’d look forward to seeing everyone, getting the music ready, standing there with the others. Quilting too — I could sit with the fabric and the colors and feel like I was making something. I’ll sit at home with the TV on low, not really watching it, just letting it make noise in the room. The wanting part feels dulled down. That’s really what brings me in, I guess — not that I hate those things, but that I don’t reach for them anymore like I used to.\n\nDoctor: Have you been forgetting appointments or conversations more than you used to?\n\nPatient: I’m not really sure. I mean, I don’t think I’m forgetting whole conversations, like someone tells me something and it’s just gone… at least I don’t think so. Sometimes people will say, “Remember I mentioned that?” and I’ll sort of have to think a minute, but then it comes back, or part of it comes back.\n\nAppointments, I try to write down, because I’ve always had to write things down. I’ve never been the kind of person who could keep everything in my head, not even when I was younger. If it’s on the calendar or somebody calls to remind me, I usually do all right.\n\nSo… more than I used to? Maybe a little, but I couldn’t swear to it. I’ve noticed I need reminders sometimes, but I don’t know if I’d call it forgetting conversations exactly.\n\nDoctor: Have the people close to you noticed that your memory or thinking has gotten worse?\n\nPatient: I don’t really know. I’m not really sure how to answer that in a clean way. I’ve had days where I felt low, especially when the days feel empty or I’m by myself too much, but I don’t know that I’d call it long stretches where I was depressed nearly every day.

It feels like the wanting is kind of dulled down.\n\nDoctor: Have you been feeling down or depressed?\n\nPatient: I don’t know if I’d call it depressed, exactly. I mean, I get quiet, and I sit around more than I used to, and some days feel kind of flat, like there’s not much spark in me. But “down” like crying all the time or feeling real sad… I’m not sure that’s it.\n\nIt’s more like things take too much out of me before I even start them. I’ll think, “I should go do that,” and then I just don’t. So I don’t know if that’s being depressed or just… I don’t know, worn out inside maybe.\n\nDoctor: Have you been having trouble with your memory?\n\nPatient: Memory… I’m not sure. I don’t think I’ve noticed anything big like that. I mean, I’ll walk into a room and forget what I went in there for, but I always figured everybody my age does that some. Or I’ll put my glasses down and then fuss around looking for them, and half the time they’re right on the table.\n\nBut as far as, you know, really not remembering people or getting lost or something… no, I don’t think so. At least nobody’s told me I’m forgetting things badly. Sometimes I don’t keep up with things because I don’t feel like doing them, but that feels different than memory to me.\n\nDoctor: About how long have you been feeling this way?\n\nPatient: It’s been… well, it didn’t just come on all at once. I’d say it’s been building since I retired from the school office. That was a little over two years ago now.\n\nAt first I thought it was just adjusting, you know, not having to get up and be somewhere, not having people coming by my desk or needing things from me. I figured I’d settle into retirement and find a rhythm. But over time it just sort of kept going that way, like I got less and less inclined to do the things I used to make myself do. So… a little over two years, I guess, if I’m being honest.\n\nDoctor: During this time, have you felt sad most days?\n\nPatient: Most days… I don’t know. I wouldn’t say sad exactly. Not like I wake up thinking, “Oh, I’m so sad,” or I’m crying into my coffee or anything like that. It’s more… blank, maybe. Quiet. Like the day is there and I’m there, but I don’t feel much about it one way or the other.\n\nSome days I do feel a little low, especially when I think about how I used to be busier and had more reason to get dressed and go out, but I’m not sure that’s sadness most days. It’s hard for me to name it. I just feel kind of slowed down and not very interested, but sad… I don’t know if that’s the right word.\n\nDoctor: Have you been having trouble managing your bills or other paperwork?\n\nPatient: Bills and paperwork… well, I try to keep the bills in the little basket by the phone, and I do usually get to them, eventually. I don’t know if I’d say it’s the bills exactly that are the worst.\n\nWhere I’ve noticed it more is with church things and the senior center. I used to help lead the choir, not just singing, but keeping track of who was coming, what music we were doing, little notes like that. Lately I’ve had to step back from a lot of that because I’ll say, “Yes, I can do that,” and then I just don’t keep up the way I used to.\n\nIt’s embarrassing, honestly, because people were used to relying on me. I’ve never been the kind of person who could keep everything in my head, not even when I was younger. Sometimes people close to me will remind me about things, but they’ve always done a bit of that, and I remind them too, so it’s hard for me to tell what’s normal and what’s something more.\n\nI guess my church friends might check on me more than before, but I don’t know if that’s because they think my thinking is worse or just because I haven’t been as dependable with things lately. They don’t say it in a mean way. It’s more like, “Don’t forget we’re meeting,” or “Do you still have what you need?” But whether that means they’ve noticed my memory… I’m not sure.\n\nI don’t want to put words in their mouths. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
I don’t think there’s been a whole two months where I felt like my old self again, no. Not really. I mean, I have better days here and there, and sometimes I’ll tell myself, “All right, tomorrow I’m going to get myself moving,” but that push just doesn’t seem to stay.

The wanting part feels dulled down. That’s really what brings me in, I guess — not that I hate those things, but that I don’t reach for them anymore like I used to.\n\nDoctor: Have you been forgetting appointments or conversations more than you used to?\n\nPatient: I’m not really sure. I mean, I don’t think I’m forgetting whole conversations, like someone tells me something and it’s just gone… at least I don’t think so. Sometimes people will say, “Remember I mentioned that?” and I’ll sort of have to think a minute, but then it comes back, or part of it comes back.\n\nAppointments, I try to write down, because I’ve always had to write things down. I’ve never been the kind of person who could keep everything in my head, not even when I was younger. If it’s on the calendar or somebody calls to remind me, I usually do all right.\n\nSo… more than I used to? Maybe a little, but I couldn’t swear to it. It might just be that there are more little things to keep track of, or I’m not paying as close attention when people are talking. I don’t want to say yes if it’s not really true. Sometimes people close to me will remind me about things, but they’ve always done a bit of that, and I remind them too, so it’s hard for me to tell what’s normal and what’s something more.\n\nI guess my church friends might check on me more than before, but I don’t know if that’s because they think my thinking is worse or just because I haven’t been as dependable with things lately. They don’t say it in a mean way. So I’d say maybe they’ve noticed I need more nudging, but I can’t really say they’ve told me my memory or thinking has gotten worse.\n\nDoctor: Has anyone close to you told you that your thinking or memory has made it hard for you to manage things on your own?\n\nPatient: No, I don’t think anyone’s told me that exactly. Not that my memory or my thinking means I can’t manage on my own. Maybe slower, and maybe I need to look at the calendar more, but I haven’t had someone close to me tell me I’m not managing. If they’re worried, they haven’t put it to me that way. I don’t think I’ve noticed anything big like that. I mean, I’ll walk into a room and forget what I went in there for, but I always figured everybody my age does that some. Or I’ll put my glasses down and then fuss around looking for them, and half the time they’re right on the table.\n\nBut as far as, you know, really not remembering people or getting lost or something… no, I don’t think so. At least nobody’s told me I’m forgetting things badly. Sometimes I don’t keep up with things because I don’t feel like doing them, but that feels different than memory to me.\n\nDoctor: About how long have you been feeling this way?\n\nPatient: It’s been… well, it didn’t just come on all at once. I’d say it’s been building since I retired from the school office. That was a little over two years ago now.\n\nAt first I thought it was just adjusting, you know, not having to get up and be somewhere, not having people coming by my desk or needing things from me. I figured I’d settle into retirement and find a rhythm. But over time it just sort of kept going that way, like I got less and less inclined to do the things I used to make myself do. So… a little over two years, I guess, if I’m being honest.\n\nDoctor: During this time, have you felt sad most days?\n\nPatient: Most days… I don’t know. I wouldn’t say sad exactly. Not like I wake up thinking, “Oh, I’m so sad,” or I’m crying into my coffee or anything like that. It’s more… blank, maybe. Quiet. Like the day is there and I’m there, but I don’t feel much about it one way or the other.\n\nSome days I do feel a little low, especially when I think about how I used to be busier and had more reason to get dressed and go out, but I’m not sure that’s sadness most days. It’s hard for me to name it. I just feel kind of slowed down and not very interested, but sad… I don’t know if that’s the right word.\n\nDoctor: Have you been having trouble managing your bills or other paperwork?\n\nPatient: Bills and paperwork… well, I try to keep the bills in the little basket by the phone, and I do usually get to them, eventually. I don’t know if I’d say it’s the bills exactly that are the worst.\n\nWhere I’ve noticed it more is with church things and the senior center. I used to help lead the choir, not just singing, but keeping track of who was coming, what music we were doing, little notes like that. And I helped with some of the senior-center projects too, making calls or bringing papers or saying I’d follow up with somebody. Lately I’ve had to step back from a lot of that because I’ll say, “Yes, I can do that,” and then I just don’t keep up the way I used to.\n\nIt’s embarrassing, honestly, because people were used to relying on me. Now some of the ladies from church check on me more than they used to, like they’ll call and say, “Did you remember we’re meeting?” or “Do you still have that paper?” They’re kind about it, but I can tell they’re watching out for me a little more. So… paperwork at home, I manage some, but keeping up with responsibilities and things I promised people has gotten harder.\n\nDoctor: Do you still enjoy things like choir or quilting when you actually do them?\n\nPatient: I suppose I do enjoy them a little once I’m there, but it’s not like it used to be. Choir used to lift me up, you know? I’d look forward to seeing everyone, getting the music ready, standing there with the others. Quilting too — I could sit with the fabric and the colors and feel like I was making something. And visiting folks, bringing something by, checking in… that used to feel natural to me.\n\nNow it’s more like… I know those things are good, and I know people are expecting me, but I just don’t have the push to get myself moving. I’ll sit at home with the TV on low, not really watching it, just letting it make noise in the room. And I’ll think, “I ought to go,” or “I said I’d be there,” but then I keep sitting there, and the time goes by.\n\nIf I do make it to choir or sit down with quilting, sometimes I’m glad I did, but it takes so much more effort than it should. The wanting part feels dulled down. That’s really what brings me in, I guess — not that I hate those things, but that I don’t reach for them anymore like I used to.\n\nDoctor: Have you been forgetting appointments or conversations more than you used to?\n\nPatient: I’m not really sure. I mean, I don’t think I’m forgetting whole conversations, like someone tells me something and it’s just gone… at least I don’t think so. Sometimes people will say, “Remember I mentioned that?” and I’ll sort of have to think a minute, but then it comes back, or part of it comes back.\n\nAppointments, I try to write down, because I’ve always had to write things down. I’ve never been the kind of person who could keep everything in my head, not even when I was younger. If it’s on the calendar or somebody calls to remind me, I usually do all right.\n\nSo… more than I used to? Maybe a little, but I couldn’t swear to it. It might just be that there are more little things to keep track of, or I’m not paying as close attention when people are talking. I don’t want to say yes if it’s not really true. I’ve noticed I need reminders sometimes, but I don’t know if I’d call it forgetting conversations exactly.\n\nDoctor: Have the people close to you noticed that your memory or thinking has gotten worse?\n\nPatient: I don’t really know. Nobody has sat me down and said, “Your memory is getting worse,” not in those words. Sometimes people close to me will remind me about things, but they’ve always done a bit of that, and I remind them too, so it’s hard for me to tell what’s normal and what’s something more.\n\nI guess my church friends might check on me more than before, but I don’t know if that’s because they think my thinking is worse or just because I haven’t been as dependable with things lately. They don’t say it in a mean way. It’s more like, “Don’t forget we’re meeting,” or “Do you still have what you need?” But whether that means they’ve noticed my memory… I’m not sure.\n\nI don’t want to put words in their mouths. I haven’t noticed them saying, “You’re confused,” or anything like that. It’s more little reminders and people being helpful. So I’d say maybe they’ve noticed I need more nudging, but I can’t really say they’ve told me my memory or thinking has gotten worse.\n\nDoctor: Has anyone close to you told you that your thinking or memory has made it hard for you to manage things on your own?\n\nPatient: No, I don’t think anyone’s told me that exactly. Not that my memory or my thinking means I can’t manage on my own. People remind me of things, like I said, and sometimes they’ll check in or ask if I’ve got something written down, but nobody has said, “You shouldn’t be doing this by yourself,” or anything like that.\n\nI mean, I still do my own things the way I know how. Maybe slower, and maybe I need to look at the calendar more, but I haven’t had someone close to me tell me I’m not managing. If they’re worried, they haven’t put it to me that way. So I’d say no… not that I know of.\n\nDoctor: Did this start after a particular stressful life change or event?\n\nPatient: I don’t know if there was one big event, like something happened on a Tuesday and then after that I was different. It wasn’t like that. It feels more like it started building after I retired from the school office, a little over two years ago now.\n\nWhen I was working, I had a routine, you know, the same place to be, people expecting me, papers and times and things laid out in a certain way. After I stopped, there wasn’t that same structure around me every day, and over time I started noticing I wasn’t quite as sharp about keeping track of things unless I wrote them down. So if you mean a stressful life change, I guess retirement was the change. I wouldn’t say it all started suddenly, but since then it’s been kind of slowly building.\n\nDoctor: In the past two years, have there been long stretches when you felt down or depressed nearly every day?\n\nPatient: I’m not really sure how to answer that in a clean way. I’ve had days where I felt low, especially when the days feel empty or I’m by myself too much, but I don’t know that I’d call it long stretches where I was depressed nearly every day.\n\nSometimes I get discouraged, yes, and I might not feel like doing much for a bit, but then there are still days I’m all right, or I talk to someone, or I get through what I need to do. So it hasn’t been like two whole years of feeling down all the time, or even months and months where every day was like that. At least, not the way I understand what you’re asking.\n\nI guess I’d say no, not long stretches nearly every day. More off and on, if anything.\n\nDoctor: Have you gotten lost in a place that should have been familiar to you?\n\nPatient: No… I don’t think so. Not lost, like I didn’t know where I was in a place I should know. I mean, sometimes I’ll pause for a minute and think, “Now which aisle was that?” if I’m in a store, or I might take a little longer remembering where something is, but that’s not the same as being lost, I don’t think.\n\nAround places I know, like near home or the regular places I go, I’ve been okay. I haven’t had that scary feeling of not knowing how to get back or not recognizing where I am. If it happened, I think it would have upset me enough that I’d remember it. So, no, not that I’ve noticed.\n\nDoctor: Have you been feeling worthless or like you’ve let people down?\n\nPatient: I wouldn’t say worthless, no. I don’t really sit there thinking I’m no good or that I’ve ruined things for everybody. I mean, I can get frustrated with myself, sure, especially if I forget something small or if I feel like I’m not keeping up the way I used to. Then I might think, “Oh, come on, why can’t you just do that?” But that feels more like being annoyed with myself than feeling worthless.\n\nAs for letting people down… maybe sometimes I worry I’m not as useful as I used to be, if that makes sense. When you’ve worked a long time and then you’re not doing that anymore, it’s easy to wonder what you’re contributing. But I don’t think I feel like I’ve failed everyone or anything like that. Not in a heavy, constant way. It comes and goes, more like little thoughts than something I believe all the time.\n\nDoctor: During the past two years, has there been a period of at least two months when you felt your usual self again, without this flat, slowed-down feeling?\n\nPatient: I don’t think there’s been a whole two months where I felt like my old self again, no. So… a little over two years, I guess, if I’m being honest.\n\nDoctor: During this time, have you felt sad most days?\n\nPatient: Most days… I don’t know. I wouldn’t say sad exactly. Not like I wake up thinking, “Oh, I’m so sad,” or I’m crying into my coffee or anything like that. It’s more… blank, maybe. Quiet. Like the day is there and I’m there, but I don’t feel much about it one way or the other.\n\nSome days I do feel a little low, especially when I think about how I used to be busier and had more reason to get dressed and go out, but I’m not sure that’s sadness most days. It’s hard for me to name it. I just feel kind of slowed down and not very interested, but sad… I don’t know if that’s the right word.\n\nDoctor: Have you been having trouble managing your bills or other paperwork?\n\nPatient: Bills and paperwork… well, I try to keep the bills in the little basket by the phone, and I do usually get to them, eventually. I don’t know if I’d say it’s the bills exactly that are the worst.\n\nWhere I’ve noticed it more is with church things and the senior center. I used to help lead the choir, not just singing, but keeping track of who was coming, what music we were doing, little notes like that. And I helped with some of the senior-center projects too, making calls or bringing papers or saying I’d follow up with somebody. Lately I’ve had to step back from a lot of that because I’ll say, “Yes, I can do that,” and then I just don’t keep up the way I used to.\n\nIt’s embarrassing, honestly, because people were used to relying on me. Now some of the ladies from church check on me more than they used to, like they’ll call and say, “Did you remember we’re meeting?” or “Do you still have that paper?” They’re kind about it, but I can tell they’re watching out for me a little more. So… paperwork at home, I manage some, but keeping up with responsibilities and things I promised people has gotten harder.\n\nDoctor: Do you still enjoy things like choir or quilting when you actually do them?\n\nPatient: I suppose I do enjoy them a little once I’m there, but it’s not like it used to be. Choir used to lift me up, you know? I’d look forward to seeing everyone, getting the music ready, standing there with the others. Quilting too — I could sit with the fabric and the colors and feel like I was making something. I’ll sit at home with the TV on low, not really watching it, just letting it make noise in the room. I’ve never been the kind of person who could keep everything in my head, not even when I was younger. If it’s on the calendar or somebody calls to remind me, I usually do all right.\n\nSo… more than I used to? Maybe a little, but I couldn’t swear to it. Nobody has sat me down and said, “Your memory is getting worse,” not in those words.
